article.body:
This week’s blog is part explanation (of a particularly curly part of our visa process) and part testimonial (having successfully navigated that curly part). For some applicants, who have reached the end of the road with their application, the bastion of last resort, the final draw of the bow, the frayed end of the rope is a request to the Minister of Immigration.

But how exactly does a request to the Minister work and what are the chances of it being successful? Well these are tricky questions to answer, but we will do our best. Just bear in mind that if you end up in this situation, it absolutely pays to seek professional assistance - largely because even though anyone can file such a request (technically), not every one should. Knowing whether this is an avenue worth pursuing is not a science but a good adviser will give you a realistic appraisal of your chances and whether it is worth spending the time and money to tackle this particular mountain.

#### **A Ministerial Request**

The Minister, being the “big cheese” in the immigration process, essentially has the power to grant anyone, any visa, for any reason. There is in fact a specific section of the Act (Section 61) that allows the Minister to grant people a Visa even if they are here unlawfully. There are a couple of caveats to this, in that the individual can’t have a deportation order in force or be subject to a removal order. For the most part, this power (Section 61) is delegated down to INZ and a specialist team that manages these requests. For most applicants filing a “Section 61” with INZ is their first port of call if they are unlawful. However, even if that process with INZ fails, nothing stops someone going to the Minister under that same section and requesting the same thing. In some cases the Minister can bring a more objective view to the situation, particularly where INZ might not have exercised balanced judgement.

**How Does It Work?**

Requests to the Minister are incredibly complex things to prepare and you have to have good grounds to make the request.

The Minister’s discretion doesn’t necessarily stop with those who are unlawful. I have assisted applicants to ask for all sorts of things, including waiving the age limited for the Skilled Migrant Category, including children who are too old to be dependent and asking for exceptions to a variety of other Resident and Temporary Visa criteria. The Minister has fairly broad powers in this respect and so if there are good grounds to make the request, it can be a viable avenue. However that doesn’t mean that every situation is worthy and certainly there is no guarantee of success. Remember the Minister has to balance the positives of granting a visa over the negatives and so you have to have a good reason to make such a request.

The actual request itself is made electronically (or you can use the post) and it is usually the Associate Minister who considers these, rather than the actual Minister. In addition, the Minister’s office is staffed with people who will pull together the details, and usually make a recommendation to the Minister, who will then make the final call. So in fact your request is not necessarily being looked at by the Minister personally.

With all of this in mind, making a request to the Minister is not something you want to do on your own. Pleading your case, by yourself can often lead to the request being unbalanced and having outside help, can ensure that your request (if it is worthwhile) is presented in the right way. It is also good to get a second opinion as to whether your request has merit- just because you can, doesn’t always mean you should. You also need to ensure that you have tried all other avenues, because the Minister will often turn away a request, if there is another avenue through INZ, that you haven’t yet tackled.

#### **Making A Request**

There is no set formula to making a request with the Minister, because everyone’s situation is different and of course, each person will have a different preference to how they present their arguments. However there are some guidelines, I have picked up over the years, having presented many of these, and achieving a very good strike rate. Not every request I have filed has been successful, but more than 80% have, largely because I chose those battles carefully.

**Balancing The Pros & Cons**

Preparing a Ministerial request requires balance between the positives and the negatives. It requires skill and experience to be done properly.

**Is it worth it?**

A lot of people believe they have a case to present to the Minister, but in fact less than half of the people I speak to about these situations, would have the right circumstances. Ultimately your situation has to be exceptional and there has to be a “hook” for the Minister to be able to hang their decision on. This is particularly common for parents, where the children want them to be able to stay here, but there are no immediate visa options. As compelling as that situation might be, these requests are rarely successful, unless there are other factors at play. So before you put pen to paper or fire up the keyboard, think carefully as to whether your request has merit.

**What’s in it for New Zealand?**

All too often, applicants focus on what is in it for them, yet realistically, the Minister has to consider what is in the interests of everyone and that includes New Zealand. This is balanced by any risks involved. So if you can demonstrate why the Minister’s intervention has a positive effect on New Zealand more generally (whether it be a social benefit, or economic one) that will aid your cause. It is also good to balance your representations and if you have messed something up, take ownership for it, but then demonstrate why having a Visa is going to lead to a positive outcome for you and the country.

**Can you prove it.**

Whatever you claim in your request has to be backed up by good, solid evidence, although bear in mind that you want to make sure the evidence tells the right story. Letters of support are useful, but not as useful as simple, relevant evidence to explain your case (and to show the benefit in considering the request favorably).

**Cut the waffle.**

Given the Minister has a lot of these requests to consider, you need to be able to explain your situation clearly and concisely. I have seen plenty of very lengthy, wordy requests full of “hitherto” and “wherefor” which might sound eloquent (and like you have a big brain) but are more about the words, and less about the actual situation. Explain your self clearly, with only the relevant facts and then a clear request as to the solution you are seeking.

There are of course a lot of other considerations when preparing a request to the Minister, but these are some of the key ones. Remember this is not necessarily a process you want to tackle on your own and so having an objective (and experienced) third party to steer the ship is strongly recommended.

#### **Our Story**

Now that you know how it all works, we can explain our recent example, where we were able to assist a client in approaching the Minister for intervention. The situation was somewhat complicated (as they usually are), but in this case we had a New Zealand citizen in a relationship with an applicant who had two children - one from a former relationship and one between the NZ citizen and the applicant.

Unfortunately for this couple, when the applicant originally arrived and applied for various visas to stay in New Zealand,  she failed to declare her relationship with her NZ partner. Finally, when the couple applied for a visa based on that relationship, INZ penalised her for not having made that relationship declaration when she applied for those earlier visas.

There was actually a very simple explanation for that non-declaration and one that catches a fair few people out. There were also issues relating to the paternity of the couple’s child, which had to be sorted out, but overall it was a bit of a mess and it left mum and the two children in New Zealand unlawfully.

We initially approached INZ with a request under Section 61 of the Act (for those here without a Visa) but we weren’t overly surprised when INZ declined that, given they were essentially arbitrating their own decision on the previous application. Remember however that we needed to be able to show that we had exhausted all available options.

So it was off to the Minister we went, with a very clear explanation as to the circumstances and a relatively simple request to give this family a chance to set things straight. It took a fairly long time to come through, but this week the Minister agreed with our arguments, granting the applicant a six month Work Visa and Student and Visitor Visas for the children. More interestingly, the Minister instructed INZ to disregard their earlier concerns over the non-declaration, for any future applications this client might wish to make. That then makes those future applications a lot easier to deal with.

A massive win for them, even if it required us having to take the path of last resort.

If you are stuck in a visa situation that looks almost impossible to get out of, or you simply don’t know where to go next, get in touch. We can give you a clear explanation as to the options that might be available and the viability of them (even the ones that aren’t obvious).

Until next week!
article.author: Paul Janssen

article.title: More Questions. Less Certainty.
article.summary: I was going to enlist the help of spider man in the image for this article, because the content relates very clearly to a certain “sense” you develop as an adviser, over years of working with applicants, Immigration New Zealand and everyone else who plays a part in the process. However, copyright rules prevented me from bringing the masked web slinger in to help.
article.body:
I was going to enlist the help of a friendly neighbourhood spider man in the image for this article, because the content relates very clearly to that uncanny “sense” you develop as an adviser, over years of working with applicants, Immigration New Zealand and everyone else who plays a part in the process. However, copyright rules prevented me from bringing the masked web slinger in to the frame.

However that “spidey-sense” or the immigration equivalent of it, “visa-sense” perhaps, is most definitely tingling for me and for reasons that most applicants would be completely unaware of. Most people applying for a visa approach this process within a narrow period of time and therefore don’t see how the process, or rather the processing, changes over a much longer period. Twenty-five years in the industry and counting, gives me a different view.

We have published immigration instructions (when the website works), application forms and document checklists, all of which are designed to give us a framework for understanding what an applicant needs to demonstrate in order to qualify. What is harder to measure is the approach taken to assessing the evidence once it arrives and more specifically how that approach changes based on so many different factors, most of which are not made obvious to potential applicants.

How much reassurance and evidence is enough? What weight does an officer give to an explanation or a particular document? When does an understandable gap become a reason to doubt the whole application and turn it down? That is where the immigration pendulum comes into play and how far that pendulum swings can be frighteningly hard to predict.

Having worked in this system for so many years, my impression is that processing moves through periods of greater pragmatism and periods of much greater caution. At present, it feels as though the pendulum has swung firmly towards caution and in some cases a tad further.

Requests for further information seem more pedantic, minor issues attract considerable attention, and declines feel more prominent. On top of that, it feels like officers are rushing to reach a conclusion, without grappling with the issues, or potentially assessing every item of evidence in totality.

I am deliberately describing an impression of course. Our caseload is not the entire immigration system, and professional frustration is not a statistical measure, but having a fairly good connection to many other professionals in the industry, that impression seems to be fairly widespread.

The question then is why do we see these shifts and what can aspiring applicants do to avoid being caught out by them.

#### **When the Atmosphere Changes**

An adviser’s gut feeling usually comes from reading applications, requests and decisions day after day. We talk to and deal with INZ officers and managers over a variety of applications and we get to see how those officers deal with similar applications. Over time, you develop a sense of which questions address a real weakness and which leave you wondering what, precisely, the officer is trying to work out.

One difficult application tells us very little about the wider system, however a recurring sense that ordinary evidence is being treated with increasing suspicion, or rather one group of applicants or one visa category is being singled out, is harder to ignore and that is exactly what the current environment feels like, at least for some visa categories.

Any examination in to subject matter like this, needs to include the work we do as an industry. Perhaps the evidence could have been clearer or the applications better prepared. Perhaps an officer has identified a concern that has been missed or perhaps the applications and applicants reaching us are becoming more complicated.

Those are all legitimate possibilities, however so is a change in the organisation’s tolerance for uncertainty and risk. I have no doubt that risk factors are evolving much more quickly than they ever have, but equally, so too must our response to that evolution, which shouldn’t include a sledgehammer and a walnut.

I have sometimes wondered whether election cycles and periods of heightened political attention to immigration play a part in these swings. Elections have a habit of making people think differently about what lies ahead, and immigration rarely stays out of the political conversation for long. Over the years, I have noticed changes in the processing atmosphere around some of those periods, although timing alone does not establish what is driving them.

What interests me is whether that wider uncertainty filters through into a more cautious approach to individual applications. It is a fair question to ask, particularly when the published requirements appear unchanged but the evidence needed to satisfy them seems to be shifting.

The real question for applicants however, is how these changes impact on their process and potential outcomes, particularly within certain visa categories.

#### **Please Prove it Again**

A recent student visa letter I reviewed for another adviser, illustrates the concern and highlights how caution in one space, can create a ripple effect of poor decision making processes that impact on a much larger pool of applicants. In this particular scenario where the applicant was applying for a further Student Visa, the officer acknowledged that the applicant had completed a New Zealand Graduate Diploma taught in English.

The applicant is now proposing to undertake a master’s qualification and yet the letter from INZ nevertheless sought an English language test result or confirmation that a test had been booked, with a response required within five working days.

There is of course a legitimate question from INZ in all of this. A master’s programme can have different demands from earlier study, and completing one qualification does not automatically establish readiness for every subsequent programme.

However completed study in English, in a country where English is a key medium of instruction, is also evidence and it deserves a meaningful place in that assessment.

The letter leaves me wanting a clearer explanation of what weight has been given to that achievement, what specific gap remains, and why a test result or booking is the information being sought - because there was literally no rationale provided, other than the rules allowed it - incidentally rules that were made more explicit after the visa was applied for.

The education provider has a role here too. INZ’s offer-of-place instructions require confirmation that the provider has assessed the prospective student’s English proficiency and academic capability to succeed in the programme. Where that assessment has been supplied, it should form part of the reasoning alongside the applicant’s previous study.

So why the overly cautious approach? Again, this is partly speculation, but over recent months Student Visas have come under the spotlight because of an increased level in fraud, which has been openly reported in specific markets, along with certain private training institutes being investigated for not following the right processes. The reasons for this are just as complex, but I lay much of the blame at a Student Visa market that has been left unchecked for far too long, as well as changes to our SMC system that created a fast-track process for an NZ master’s graduate, which in turn has incentivised people to potentially exploit that opportunity.

So understandably there is a greater degree of scepticism amongst officers. However that increased caution shouldn’t replace fairness and common sense.

Yet this is where the pendulum effect becomes quite apparent. In trying to fix one problem, the system inadvertently creates many more, and the biggest one we can see right now, is the market responding by deciding that other countries might offer a more practical pathway.

Everything we do in the immigration space, sends a signal and yet we forget how important those signals are. It is really easy to turn off the immigration tap, far harder to turn it back on again.

#### **The Cost of Another Question**

A request for further information can look quite modest from behind a desk, particularly when the person asking for it is simply following standard operating procedure. Sending the letter, with a deadline of a few days is neither here nor there, when you aren’t the applicant and you haven’t paid the fees, gathered the documents and put your hopes and dreams in to the application.

For the applicant, it can mean finding a test appointment at short notice, paying another set of fees, contacting a former institution or seeking another explanation from an education provider. It can also mean another period of uncertainty while study, employment and family plans remain in limbo.

Sometimes that work is necessary and applicants need to establish that they qualify, and INZ needs to investigate genuine concerns that might undermine that eligibility.

Every additional request should nevertheless have a clear purpose and be backed up by reasoning that can be scrutinised. It should help resolve something material to the decision and be based on something more than “we are not satisfied”, which is not much of an explanation at all.

Asking for more documents can become an easy response to uncertainty and risk, especially if the harder and more lengthy task, requires weighing the evidence already available and making a reasoned decision.

My concern is that an organisation trying to reduce risk and fix a problem in one place, can gradually become less comfortable exercising judgment and dispensing fairness in another. All the while this reactionary approach creates, trickle-down issues in many more places. The files get thicker while the underlying question remains unanswered.

INZ’s own fairness instructions provide a useful reference point, because they require officers to consider the facts with an open mind towards relevant evidence and to distinguish facts from assumptions and opinion. Those principles matter particularly when an application does not fit a familiar pattern.

However that fairness principle seems to become a little thin and hard to justify when you just start asking every applicant for extra documents because of the risk factors a particular visa category or profile of applicant might be prone to.

#### **Listening to the Warning**

I cannot offer a graph proving that INZ has become more risk averse across the board and nor can I demonstrate that politics explains the processing atmosphere creating the tingling “visa-sense”. However what I can say and I suspect my industry colleagues would agree with, is that there is a very different approach to processing being taken for various visa pathways, that is very hard to ignore.

The world is of course a far more complicated place and the ability for fraud to be a factor in a visa application has increased exponentially with the rise of very powerful AI tools. However the collateral damage when everyone is considered suspicious or at least an entire group of applicants or everyone applying for a particular type of visa, is that good quality applicants end up under the same lens.

That consequence goes much further than just that applicant or group of applicants and it is a consequence that may not be readily visible when assessing an individual application. It is easy to tighten the tap and turn off the flow, much harder to make it come back again when suddenly you want more students, more workers, more visitors or more skilled migrants. I have written about the idea of signals before, and its something our immigration system is particularly bad at understanding and managing.

Applicants need clear requirements, careful assessment and reasons they can understand, which in turn creates a system that delivers certainty. That doesn’t mean every application will be approved and it also doesn’t negate the fact we need good risk management, but increased scrutiny shouldn’t come at the expense of fairness and common sense. When further evidence is necessary to decide an application, applicants or the advisers assisting them should be able to see what question it will answer.

For aspiring applicants, it is easy to think that it is all just too hard, but I would caveat all of the above with the fact that the vast majority of good quality applicants have nothing to fear. The processing might be more prickly and pedantic, but if you qualify, then some good advocacy and navigation will give you a much better chance of success.

The pendulum may be difficult to measure. The consequences of its movement are much easier to feel.

Until next week…

Paul Janssen

**Director, Turner Hopkins Immigration Specialists**
